items.sentence: The girl opened the window.

items.sentence: My mother baked a cake yesterday.
items.rule: Baked is transitive: its object is a cake. Yesterday tells when; it is not an object.

items.sentence: The children sang a song loudly.
items.rule: Sang is transitive here: its object is a song. In "The children sang loudly", there is no object.

items.sentence: It rained heavily. However, the match went on.
items.rule: However joins two ideas that pull apart.

items.sentence: He practised daily. Therefore, he improved quickly.
items.rule: Therefore shows the result.

items.sentence: She was tired. [Therefore], she kept working.
items.rule: However shows that the second idea is unexpected.

items.sentence: The opposite of generous is [kind].

items.sentence: A word that means the same as brave is [timid].
items.rule: A synonym is a word of the same meaning: brave, courageous.

items.sentence: Hot is to cold as day is to [sun].

items.sentence: The opposite of ancient is [old].
items.rule: An antonym is a word of opposite meaning: ancient, modern.

items.sentence: Glove is to hand as sock is to [shoe].
items.rule: An analogy matches pairs: a glove goes on a hand, a sock goes on a foot.

items.rule: Opened has an object, the window, so it is transitive.

items.sentence: The birds flew away.

items.sentence: He wrote a long letter.

items.sentence: She was reluctant to speak, and looked at the floor until the teacher asked twice.

items.rule: She had to be asked twice, so she was unwilling.

items.sentence: Rain was scarce that year, and the wells nearly ran dry.

items.rule: The wells nearly ran dry, so there was little rain.

items.rule: The rhyme with sky and high points to goodbye.

items.sentence: Ravi asked me where I was going.

items.sentence: Last week she said that she [will] visit us soon.
items.rule: In reported speech "will" becomes "would".

items.sentence: The teacher told us to open our books.

items.sentence: The boy who won the race is my cousin.

items.rule: After "to", use "me": to Ravi and me.

items.rule: The reflexive form of "we" is "ourselves".

items.sentence: He cut [hisself] while peeling the mango.
items.rule: The reflexive form of "he" is "himself".

items.sentence: I hurt [me] when I fell off the bicycle.
items.rule: When the doer and the receiver are the same person, use the reflexive: myself.

items.sentence: The students finished [his] work early.
items.rule: A plural noun takes a plural pronoun: the students, their.

items.sentence: The puppy wagged [their] tail.
items.rule: One animal takes "its".

items.sentence: Meena and Ravi forgot [her] books.
items.rule: Two people joined by "and" take "their".

items.sentence: Yesterday she opened the door and [walks] in.
items.rule: "Yesterday" sets the past, so keep to it: opened, walked.

items.sentence: Last Sunday we went to the beach and [swim] all day.
items.rule: "Last Sunday" sets the past, so keep to it: went, swam.

items.sentence: Every day he picks up the bat and [hit] the ball.
items.rule: "Every day" sets the present, so keep to it: picks, hits.

items.sentence: The girl whose bag was lost is crying.
items.rule: "Whose" adds information about what belongs to a person.

items.sentence: The house where I was born is very old.
items.rule: "Where" adds information about a place.

items.sentence: I know the girl who painted this picture.
items.rule: "Who" adds information about a person.

items.sentence: She asked whether I had finished my work.
items.rule: A yes or no question is reported with "whether" or "if", in statement order.

items.sentence: Yesterday he said that he [can] swim across the lake.
items.rule: In reported speech "can" becomes "could".

items.sentence: When the bell rang, the children [run] out of the class.
items.rule: "Rang" sets the past, so keep to it: rang, ran.

items.sentence: The birds built [its] nest in our mango tree.
items.rule: A plural noun takes a plural pronoun: the birds, their.

items.sentence: When it rained, we stayed inside.

items.sentence: Although she was tired, Meena finished her work.
items.rule: The main clause can stand alone: Meena finished her work. "Although she was tired" cannot.

items.sentence: The boy who won smiled proudly.

items.sentence: We will go out if the rain stops.
items.rule: The main clause can stand alone: we will go out. "If the rain stops" cannot.

items.sentence: The children played IN THE GARDEN.

items.rule: A clause has a subject and a verb: the sun set.

items.sentence: She spoke WITH GREAT CARE.

items.rule: A phrase has no subject with its own verb: with great care.

items.sentence: I will wait IF YOU ARE LATE.

items.rule: A clause has a subject and a verb: you are.

items.sentence: The wind whispered through the trees.

items.sentence: The classroom was a zoo.

items.rule: A metaphor says one thing is another, without like or as.

items.sentence: Seven silver swans swam silently.
items.question: Which figure of speech is this?
items.rule: Alliteration repeats the same first sound: seven silver swans.

items.sentence: Her smile was sunshine.
items.question: Which figure of speech is this?
items.rule: A metaphor says one thing is another: her smile was sunshine.

items.sentence: The stars danced in the sky.
items.question: Which figure of speech is this?
items.rule: Personification gives a human action to a thing: the stars danced.

items.sentence: The baker stopped making doughnuts, tired of the hole business.
items.question: Which figure of speech is this?
items.rule: A pun plays on two meanings or two words that sound alike: hole and whole.

items.sentence: A letter to the head teacher asking for a day off.

items.rule: A formal letter uses polite, complete and exact language.
right: I request you to grant me leave for one day.
wrong: Give me a day off, okay?

items.sentence: A message to a close friend about a film.
items.question: Which sentence fits?
items.rule: With a friend, friendly everyday language is right; stiff language sounds odd.
right: That film was great, you must see it!
wrong: I wish to inform you that the film was satisfactory.
Kindly be advised of the merits of the film.

items.sentence: A notice on the school board about a meeting.
items.question: Which sentence fits?
items.rule: A notice is formal: it gives what, where and when, plainly.
right: The meeting will be held in the hall at ten o'clock.
wrong: Hey guys, meeting in the hall, be there!
You lot had better turn up at ten.

items.sentence: A thank-you note to your grandmother.
items.question: Which sentence fits?
items.rule: A note to family is warm and polite: neither stiff nor curt.
right: Thank you so much for the lovely present.
wrong: Receipt of the present is hereby acknowledged.

items.sentence: It was raining. We went out.
items.question: Which sentence joins the two correctly?
items.rule: Although joins two ideas that pull apart; it is not used together with but.
right: Although it was raining, we went out.
wrong: Although it was raining, but we went out.
It was raining although we went out.

items.sentence: The boy won the prize. He is my cousin.
items.question: Which sentence joins the two correctly?
items.rule: Who joins a sentence about a person to the noun it describes.
right: The boy who won the prize is my cousin.
wrong: The boy is my cousin who he won the prize.
The boy which won the prize is my cousin.

items.sentence: She was tired. She finished her work.
items.question: Which sentence joins the two correctly?
items.rule: But joins two ideas that pull apart, making a compound sentence.
right: She was tired, but she finished her work.
wrong: She was tired, so she finished her work.
She was tired because she finished her work.

items.sentence: I missed the bus. I woke up late.
items.question: Which sentence joins the two correctly?
items.rule: Because joins a result to its reason.
right: I missed the bus because I woke up late.
wrong: I missed the bus, so I woke up late.
I missed the bus although I woke up late.

items.sentence: The house stood silent, its windows dark, and a cold wind rattled the gate.
items.question: What is the mood of these lines?
items.rule: Silent, dark, cold and rattled all build an uneasy mood.

items.sentence: Lanterns glowed along the street, drums rolled, and children raced past with sweets in their hands.
items.question: What is the mood of these lines?
items.rule: Lanterns, drums and children with sweets build a festive mood.

items.sentence: The swing hung still. Her shoes were by the door, where she had left them a year ago.
items.question: What is the mood of these lines?
items.rule: A still swing and shoes untouched for a year build a sad mood.

items.sentence: Of course the bus was late. It is always late on the one day I am early.
items.question: What is the tone of the speaker?
items.rule: Of course and always show a speaker who is mildly annoyed and joking about it.

items.sentence: First, wash the rice. Next, boil the water. Finally, add the rice and cover the pot.
items.question: How is this text built?
items.rule: First, next and finally mark steps in order.
wrong: As a problem and its answer
As a comparison of two things

items.sentence: The village well ran dry every summer. So the farmers dug a pond to store the rain.

items.rule: The text states a problem, then what was done about it.

wrong: As a comparison of two things

right: As a comparison of two things
wrong: As a problem and its answer

items.rule: As a result links what happened to its cause.

wrong: As a comparison of two things

items.question: What does this show about the speaker?
items.rule: Naturally and I always do show someone who boasts.

items.sentence: The bridge was [build] many years ago.
items.rule: The passive uses the past participle: was built.

items.sentence: The letters were [wrote] by the secretary.
items.rule: The passive uses the past participle: were written.

items.sentence: The match was cancelled because of the rain.
items.rule: In the passive, the thing acted on comes first: the match was cancelled.

items.sentence: The results will be announced tomorrow.

items.sentence: If I [was] you, I would apologise.
items.rule: For something unreal, use were: if I were you.

items.sentence: If she had studied, she would have [pass] the test.
items.rule: After would have, use the past participle: would have passed.

items.sentence: If it rains tomorrow, we [would] cancel the picnic.
items.rule: A real possibility takes the present, then will: if it rains, we will cancel.

items.sentence: If I had known, I would have come earlier.
items.rule: For a past that did not happen: if with had, then would have.

items.sentence: Unless you hurry, you will miss the bus.
items.rule: Unless means if not: unless you hurry.

items.sentence: You should have [tell] me the truth.
items.rule: After should have, use the past participle: should have told.

items.sentence: He must have [forget] the meeting.
items.rule: After must have, use the past participle: must have forgotten.

items.sentence: They might have missed the last train.
items.rule: Might have with a past participle is a guess about the past.

items.sentence: She enjoys [swim] in the sea.

items.sentence: He avoided [answer] the question.
items.rule: After avoid, use the -ing form: avoided answering.

items.sentence: I look forward to [meet] you.
items.rule: After look forward to, use the -ing form: to meeting you.

items.sentence: We agreed to meet at the station.
items.rule: After agree, use to with the verb: agreed to meet.

items.sentence: She likes reading, painting and [cook].
items.rule: Items in a list take the same form: reading, painting and cooking.

items.sentence: He spoke clearly, calmly and [confident].
items.rule: Items in a list take the same form: clearly, calmly and confidently.

items.sentence: The job needs patience, accuracy and good humour.
items.rule: Items in a list take the same form: three nouns.

items.sentence: I will call you WHEN I ARRIVE.

items.sentence: The boy WHO WON THE RACE is my cousin.

wrong: It tells when: an adverb clause
It is the thing known or said: a noun clause

items.sentence: I know THAT SHE IS HONEST.

wrong: It describes a noun: an adjective clause
It tells why: an adverb clause

items.sentence: We stayed inside BECAUSE IT WAS RAINING.

It is the thing known or said: a noun clause

It is the thing known or said: a noun clause

items.sentence: The new library was [open] by the mayor last week.
